notes: The Skarl Bridge's one voice (world life, Briarwold): the foreman who pays blood-price at the middle of the bridge. Gives core:quest/the_price_at_the_middle and hears its decision.

greet.speaker: Tosk ko-Skarl
greet.text: Tosk, of the Skarl. You are standing in the Wold. I am standing on the middle stone, which is in both. Step on it if you like. It does not make you anything.

topic_1.speaker: Tosk ko-Skarl
topic_1.text: Blood-price. A month's. For a boy the clan's spoil buried under the tor in the thaw of 1033. The clan's law says a death is a debt and a debt is paid. So I pay it. — Nobody takes it. The Woodfolk say nothing. The rain takes it into the Skarl Water, a coin at a time, and I come back with more. It is not a price if nobody takes it. I know that. I pay it anyway.

topic_2.speaker: Tosk ko-Skarl
topic_2.text: Because this side is custom and that side is law, and the middle is the only stone in the world where I am standing in both. The clan put me out of nothing. The Wold did not take me in. I have a stone.

topic_3.speaker: Tosk ko-Skarl
topic_3.text: A tin vein we followed into the tor above the Colley woman's hearth. Two years. Good tin, and a good adit, square, timbered the clan way. We heaped the spoil on the slope because it was quicker. It was quicker. — The clan went home. The weavers came up out of Blackgill and took the galleries. Something big went to the bottom. I hear it moving when the wind is right.

hub.speaker: Tosk ko-Skarl
hub.text: Speak. The water is loud here; I will listen harder.

choices.text: What is the silver on the parapet?
Why the middle of the bridge?
What is the Skarl Delving?
The silver on the bridge. Can the debt be paid some other way?
I have the boy's whistle. It was in the web at the bottom of the shaft.
Goodbye.

bye.speaker: Tosk ko-Skarl
bye.text: Mind the middle stone. It is worn in the centre, from me.

q_the_price_at_the_middle_offer.speaker: Tosk ko-Skarl
q_the_price_at_the_middle_offer.text: Some other way. — The Woodfolk bury under moss, a named moss for every one, tended until nobody is left who remembers. The boy has a moss. Orla Colley keeps it by her door. There is nothing under it. There has been nothing under it for eleven years, because he is under the tor, in the dark, with the weavers. — I cannot go in. I would need the Wold's leave, and the Wold gives none and refuses none. You are not the clan. Ask his mother. If she does not say no, go down, and bring out whatever there is of him.

choices.text: I'll ask her.
Not now.

q_the_price_at_the_middle_accept.speaker: Tosk ko-Skarl
q_the_price_at_the_middle_accept.text: Her hearth is under the tor, where the smoke is. She has never been to this bridge. Do not tell her I sent you. — Tell her I sent you. She should know who is asking.

q_the_price_at_the_middle_decide.speaker: Tosk ko-Skarl
q_the_price_at_the_middle_decide.text: *He steps off the middle stone for the first time, and looks at it in your hand, and steps back on.* — A whistle. He whittled. The men gave him the offcuts from the timbering. — Eleven years I have paid silver to the river, and it was a whistle. — It is not mine to say where it goes. I have wanted to say it every month. You say it.

choices.text: To Orla Colley, to lie under his moss.
To you, to carry to Skarlow and put his name in the Rope-Song.
On the parapet here, at the middle, with the silver.
Let me think on it.

q_the_price_at_the_middle_decide_under_t.speaker: Tosk ko-Skarl
q_the_price_at_the_middle_decide_under_t.text: Under the moss. — Yes. That is where the Wold keeps its dead, and he was the Wold's. I will not go with you. I will stand here and I will know when it is done, because the smoke from her clamp will change. It does, when she is glad. The men used to say so.

q_the_price_at_the_middle_decide_the_rop.speaker: Tosk ko-Skarl
q_the_price_at_the_middle_decide_the_rop.text: In the Song. — A woodfolk boy's name in the clans' own verses, sung at every moot until the rope rots. The Woodfolk will not like it. The clan will like it less. — I will carry it up. I will sing the verse myself if they will not, and they will not, and I will. Thank you.

q_the_price_at_the_middle_decide_at_the_.speaker: Tosk ko-Skarl
q_the_price_at_the_middle_decide_at_the_.text: Here. — Where both countries can see it. The Woodfolk walk past on this side and the clan on that, and there it is, on the middle stone, a boy's whistle and a heap of rained-on silver. — It is not a price and it is not a moss. It is the truth, left where anybody can read it. Perhaps that is what the middle stone was for.

greetings.text: The smoke from the Colley clamp has been white since you went up. The men were right. — I have stopped paying. I still stand here. Habit, or the view.
They let the verse into the Song. Not the first night. The fourth. Somebody in Skarlow had been waiting eleven years for somebody else to ask.
People stop at the middle now. Both sides. They look at it and they do not touch it and they go on. Nobody has said a word to me about it, which in the Wold is a great deal.

notes: The burner at Colley's Hearth under the Skarl tor (world life, Briarwold), and a merchant of charcoal. Davy Colley's mother; the first stage of core:quest/the_price_at_the_middle closes on her line q_price_leave.

greet.speaker: Orla Colley
greet.text: Stand off the clamp. It's fretful when there's somebody new. — Charcoal, is it? Fallen wood only, by the verderers' leave, and it burns clean.

topic_1.speaker: Orla Colley
topic_1.text: My boy's. Star-moss, hair-moss, feather-moss, cushion-moss. Davy. — There's nothing under it. There's a list of what it's for in a sack inside the door, if you want to read it. Most people don't.

topic_2.speaker: Orla Colley
topic_2.text: No. — The clan's man stands on it with his silver. He's stood there eleven years. I know. I can see the bridge from the top of the tor on a clear day. — I don't want the silver. I never said so. It's not custom to say so.

topic_3.speaker: Orla Colley
topic_3.text: Quiet. Weavers in the adit after dark, and they come down to the clamp for the warmth sometimes and I let them, and they go back up. — At night, when the draught's up the shaft, I can hear his whistle. One note. He never could play it properly.

choices.text: Whose is the moss by the door?
Do you ever go to the bridge?
What's it like, living under the delving?
Tosk ko-Skarl sent me. He wants to go into the delving for your son, and can't without the Wold's leave.
Goodbye.

bye.speaker: Orla Colley
bye.text: Mind the clamp on your way.

q_price_leave.speaker: Orla Colley
q_price_leave.text: *She puts the twig she is whittling into the clamp and watches it catch.* — Leave. The Wold doesn't give leave. You know that, or he wouldn't have sent you. — I'll tell you what I'd tell anyone, then, and you can take it for what it's worth up there. I hear his whistle down the delving at night. There's been nothing under his moss for eleven years. I'd like there to be something. — That's not leave. That's what I'd like.

greetings.text: It's under the moss. I put it there myself with my own hands and I sang him the list. — Go on. I've a clamp to see to, and I'd like to see to it on my own.
The clan's singing him, I'm told. In Skerrish. He never had a word of it. — He'd have liked that. He liked a thing he couldn't understand.
I went to the bridge. First time. I stood at the middle and looked at it and the clan's man looked at me. Neither of us said anything. I'll go again.

notes: The Tallying Hide's hunter (world life, Briarwold): keeps the count of harts carried to the Horn Pale. Gives core:quest/custom_says_wait and hears its decision.

greet.speaker: Corra Bracken
greet.text: *She does not come down out of the oak. Her voice does.* — Two hundred and eleven. That's not a greeting, it's the count. Come round the tree where I can see you.

topic_1.speaker: Corra Bracken
topic_1.text: Harts. The poachers carry the heads east past this oak to the Horn Pale every morning, and I cut a notch for every one. A long notch for twelve tines and over. A cross for a hind. — I've run out of post twice. I've started on the tree.

topic_2.speaker: Corra Bracken
topic_2.text: Custom. The Woodfolk may not burn a poachers' camp while there are poachers in it; that's so nobody burns a man in his sleep, and it's a good custom. The factor who built the Pale knows it. He keeps them in the yard. All of them. Every night. — So nobody burns it. And nobody says anything, because that's custom too. I don't say anything either. I count.

topic_3.speaker: Corra Bracken
topic_3.text: A buying-house. Stakes and a gate, a Tallymen's man with a book, and a hedge of antlers over the door. They pay two marks the tine. They sell them in the Lantern Row at forty, with the Builders' mark burned in. Forty. I've never had forty marks in my life. I've never wanted them.

hub.speaker: Corra Bracken
hub.text: Say it. Two hundred and twelve if you're slow.

choices.text: What are you counting?
Why doesn't anyone stop them?
What is the Horn Pale?
Custom doesn't bind me. What would you have done about the Pale?
The Pale's yard is empty. The books are read. What now?
Goodbye.

bye.speaker: Corra Bracken
bye.text: Go quietly. They look up at this oak more than they did.

q_custom_says_wait_offer.speaker: Corra Bracken
q_custom_says_wait_offer.text: *She comes down, which she has not done for anybody before.* — Nothing, if I'm honest. That's the trouble with custom. — But you're not Woodfolk. — The harts are taken at the Hartswell at first light, where nobody hunts. Start there. Then find out what they're paid and what it's sold for, because I want it written down somewhere other than my tree. Then we'll see what custom says about a pale with no poachers in it.

choices.text: Start at the Hartswell. I'll go.
Not now.

q_custom_says_wait_accept.speaker: Corra Bracken
q_custom_says_wait_accept.text: First light. They'll be in the bracken on the east side, downwind. — Don't kill a hart by accident. That would be two hundred and twelve and I'd have to cut it.

q_custom_says_wait_decide.speaker: Corra Bracken
q_custom_says_wait_decide.text: *She sits on the root of her oak with the knife in her hand and does not cut anything.* — Kenard read them. I watched his face from up here. — The yard's empty. There's no poacher in it tonight, and custom has nothing to say about an empty pale, nothing at all. For the first time in three summers it's up to somebody. You brought the books. You say.

choices.text: Burn it, while it is empty.
Give the books to the knights. Let them stand at its gate.
Send the books to Tollmere, to the Tallymen's own clerks.
Let me think on it.

q_custom_says_wait_decide_burn_the_pale.speaker: Corra Bracken
q_custom_says_wait_decide_burn_the_pale.text: Burn it. — There's nobody in it. I'll carry the fire myself. I'll stand where they can see me from the Wold Water and I'll let the Tallymen's crates go up with it, and in the morning I'll cut one notch, a long one, across all the others.

q_custom_says_wait_decide_to_the_knights.speaker: Corra Bracken
q_custom_says_wait_decide_to_the_knights.text: The knights. — Kenard will put a knight on the gate by the week's end, and no poacher will walk past a Hart-Knight with a hart's head under his arm; they're not that brave. It's slower than fire. — It's kinder than fire. I'll keep counting till the count stops.

q_custom_says_wait_decide_to_the_lantern.speaker: Corra Bracken
q_custom_says_wait_decide_to_the_lantern.text: Tollmere. — Let the Lantern Row read what it's been selling. The Tallymen won't like it. The Tallymen's customers will like it less. — I'll never know what happens down there. I'll know if the heads stop coming past my oak. That's all I need to know.

greetings.text: One long notch, across all of them. I cut it that morning. The oak didn't mind.
There's a knight at the Pale's gate, leaning on his spear, looking at every sack that goes in. Nothing's gone past my oak in nine days.
A Tallymen's clerk came up the Wold Water in a hurry and went down again in a bigger one. The factor went with him. The count's stopped.

notes: The Hart-Knight who keeps the Tine Barrow's door (world life, Briarwold). The fourth stage of core:quest/custom_says_wait closes on his line q_custom_books.

greet.speaker: Kenard Hartwell
greet.text: *He is chalking a name on the forecourt stone, and finishes it, and says it aloud before he looks up.* — Tamsen. — You are welcome at the barrow by day. Go before midnight. They walk then.

topic_1.speaker: Kenard Hartwell
topic_1.text: The first knights. Forty of them. Each one named for the hart he would not kill: Ardo for the white hart, Bell for the hart of the Hollow ford, Tamsen for the hart that gored her. We wear the antlers of harts that died old, so they are remembered. That is all we are for.

topic_2.speaker: Kenard Hartwell
topic_2.text: No. — Never. Not once. The Woodfolk will not ask us, and so they believe it, and so it goes round the Wold that the knights hang the antlers of every hart they kill. We hang the antlers of every hart that dies. It is a different sentence. It is the whole difference.

topic_3.speaker: Kenard Hartwell
topic_3.text: The antlers in Tollmere. They sell them as Oroth relics, the Builders' holy things, and they put our name on the ticket. I would like them counted, and the count brought here, so that I can say the names of the harts over them. I do not know the harts' names. I will say something.

hub.speaker: Kenard Hartwell
hub.text: Ask. I have sat here nineteen years; I am not in a hurry.

choices.text: Who lies in the barrow?
Do the Hart-Knights kill harts?
What do you want counted?
Corra Bracken sent me. These are the boilers' account book and the Horn Pale's price book.
Goodbye.

bye.speaker: Kenard Hartwell
bye.text: Before midnight. I mean it kindly.

q_custom_books.speaker: Kenard Hartwell
q_custom_books.text: *He reads the boilers' book through, and the factor's, and then both again, turning the pages with the back of his gauntlet so as not to mark them.* — Two marks. Forty in the Lantern Row. The masons' marks out of the Old Quarry, burned in and called the Builders' hand. And the Hart-Knights have no standing in the Charter. — That is true. We have none. — Go back to Corra Bracken. She has counted them. She should say what is done. Tell her the knights will stand wherever she says, and that we are ashamed it took somebody who is not Woodfolk to bring us this.

greetings.text: Two hundred and eleven. Corra Bracken sent me her count. I have been saying something over each of them, a few every morning, after the knights. I will be done by the spring.

notes: The Hart-Knight kneeling at the Moot Gate Stone (world life, Briarwold): the atlas's hook, 'a Hart-Knight has knelt three days and will not say what he is waiting for'.

greet.speaker: Wystan Tine
greet.text: *He does not turn from the gate.* — Seventy-one hours. Speak low.

topic_1.speaker: Wystan Tine
topic_1.text: For the gate to say what it is. A gate is known by what comes through it. The first knights knelt here before they took the antlers, facing the gate the Hart came through. I took them twenty years ago. I am asking the gate whether it is still the same gate. — Nothing has come through. That is an answer too. I do not like it.

topic_2.speaker: Wystan Tine
topic_2.text: The Hart. So the Tine Barrow says, and Kenard Hartwell, who keeps it. Whether it came through to keep the Wold or to keep something out of it, the Barrow does not say. It is carved in stone and the stone was cut by knights who did not know either.

topic_3.speaker: Wystan Tine
topic_3.text: Water. Nothing else. — No. Not water either. Seventy-two hours is the vigil. I will drink at seventy-two.

choices.text: What are you waiting for?
What came through the gate, the first time?
Is there anything I can bring you?
Goodbye.

bye.speaker: Wystan Tine
bye.text: *He says nothing, which you understand to be goodbye.*

notes: The Sayer at the Listening Horns (world life, Briarwold), waiting for the Listeners of 1038. Gives core:quest/what_the_horns_heard and hears its decision.

greet.speaker: Merel Quill
greet.text: *She has her ear to the brass and holds up one finger, and waits, and lowers it.* — Merel Quill, of the Circle, and I'm sorry: the east horn was humming. It does, after noon. Come in, sit, don't touch the tripods.

topic_1.speaker: Merel Quill
topic_1.text: Listening. The Circle made them for the Moot's note, to hear whether it holds or shifts. The Listeners brought them here in 1038 and turned them on the northern gate instead, because the Briar is the other thing in the Wold that nobody understands. — They heard something. The last leaf of their log is under the middle horn. You can read it; it is not mine to keep.

topic_2.speaker: Merel Quill
topic_2.text: Six Sayers and a dog. Imber Vane led them; I taught him his first Saying when he was nine and he corrected my accent. Ansa Rook, the Oskel twins, a girl from Isseva called Lisse who could hear a lie across a room, and Crane, who was nobody's student and everybody's. And the dog. — They went through the northern gate. The chalk they marked it with is still on the stone.

topic_3.speaker: Merel Quill
topic_3.text: Because they will come back through the gate they went out by, and somebody should be listening when they do. — The Circle thinks I'm mad. The Circle pays for my paper. The Circle would very much like to send a second expedition and would very much like me to stop saying that the first one is still walking.

hub.speaker: Merel Quill
hub.text: The horns are listening. So am I. Go on.

choices.text: What are the horns for?
Who were the Listeners?
Why come back every summer?
What have the horns been hearing?
I've been to the beacon. Someone from the far side has been laying it.
Goodbye.

bye.speaker: Merel Quill
bye.text: Go softly past the east horn. It picks up boots.

q_what_the_horns_heard_offer.speaker: Merel Quill
q_what_the_horns_heard_offer.text: *She takes her ear from the brass, which she does not do.* — Footsteps. On the far side of the thorn, walking north along the Briar at a walker's pace, every night after the Moot's hum starts. And a dog. — Crane's dog. I would know it. — I cannot leave the horns; if they come while I'm gone I'll never forgive myself. The east horn hears it loudest where a runner of the Briar has grown out through the rampart, a mile south. The Rookhold keepers call it the Stray Thorn. Go and look. Please.

choices.text: I'll go to the Stray Thorn.
Not now.

q_what_the_horns_heard_accept.speaker: Merel Quill
q_what_the_horns_heard_accept.text: Thornhounds lie up under it, the porter says. Ivo says a great many things. Believe that one.

q_what_the_horns_heard_decide.speaker: Merel Quill
q_what_the_horns_heard_decide.text: *She listens to all of it with her ear against the east horn, as if checking it.* — Pressed-ash grain. There's no such wood in the Wold. There's no such wood in the Circle's herbals. — And 'I do', under the rule. — Somebody on the far side of the thorn is keeping a Woodfolk beacon laid, by the Woodfolk's own rule, and has been since the Firewatch fell. — I have been listening for six years. I am out of things to listen for. Tell me what to do.

choices.text: Light the beacon, so whoever is out there can see the way.
Leave it laid. Whoever lays it knows the rule.
Turn the horns from the gate and take them home. Stop listening.
Let me think on it.

q_what_the_horns_heard_decide_light_it.speaker: Merel Quill
q_what_the_horns_heard_decide_light_it.text: Light it. — The rule says fire and nothing else. — I don't care. I'll go up with Ivo tonight and put a torch to it, and the whole Wold will come with spades, and they'll find a Sayer standing by a burning beacon saying sorry. And somebody on the far side of the thorn will see it. Imber would have lit it. Imber lit everything.

q_what_the_horns_heard_decide_leave_it_l.speaker: Merel Quill
q_what_the_horns_heard_decide_leave_it_l.text: Leave it. — Yes. Whoever it is, they keep the rule better than we do. They lay it and they don't light it, every autumn, for eleven years, for a fire nobody has had. That is not a Listener. That is a keeper. — I'll write it in the log. I'll keep listening. I'll know, now, what I'm listening to.

q_what_the_horns_heard_decide_turn_the_h.speaker: Merel Quill
q_what_the_horns_heard_decide_turn_the_h.text: Stop. — *She is quiet a long time.* — The leaf says 'we will not need them'. Imber wrote that. He was right; they didn't. — Ivo, help me with the tripods. We'll turn them to the Moot, where the Circle made them to point, and carry them down in the spring. If the Listeners want me they know where the Spire is.

greetings.text: The Wold came with spades and found me, and I said sorry, and they said nothing, and stood with me and watched it burn. On the far side of the thorn, for a moment, there was a second fire.
The footsteps stopped at the beacon's knoll last night, and stood, and went on north. I wrote down how long they stood. It was the time it takes to lay a fire.
The horns are on the Moot. It hums. It holds. It's a relief, in its way, to listen to a thing that is only what it is.

notes: Merel Quill's porter at the Listening Horns (world life, Briarwold).

greet.speaker: Ivo Lantry
greet.text: Ivo Lantry, porter, Lantern Row, and no, I don't know what she's listening to, and yes, there's bread.

topic_1.speaker: Ivo Lantry
topic_1.text: Six summers I've carried her paper up here and sat by this fire and told her there's nothing. Wind in the thorn. Weavers on the brass. — Last two summers I've put my ear to the east horn when she's asleep. — There's somebody walking. That's all I'll say. And I've never said it.

topic_2.speaker: Ivo Lantry
topic_2.text: It's the four notes the east horn does, after the Moot starts. I didn't mean to learn it. — She hasn't noticed. Don't tell her. She'll want me to write it down.

topic_3.speaker: Ivo Lantry
topic_3.text: Weavers come down to the brass after dark; the horns hum and they like the hum. Thornhounds under the Stray Thorn. And the Wold folk, who look at you and say nothing, which after six summers I've come round to. It's restful.

hub.speaker: Ivo Lantry
hub.text: *He is whistling four notes and stops.* — Yes?

choices.text: What do you make of the horns?
What's the tune you whistle?
Is the Northwold dangerous?
Goodbye.

bye.speaker: Ivo Lantry
bye.text: Mind the east horn. It picks up boots. She'll tell you. She tells everyone.

notes: The eldest thorn-layer, at the Layers' Ring (world life, Briarwold). Gives core:quest/grey_under_the_green and hears its decision.

greet.speaker: Kit Laywood
greet.text: *She does not take off her gauntlets to greet you. She never does.* — Kit Laywood. We lay the thorn. You'll want to stand clear of the bundles; they bite.

topic_1.speaker: Kit Laywood
topic_1.text: Where the Thornmarch thins, we lay it thick again. You bend the runner that's there down into the thorn beside it and pin it with a hazel crook, and it roots where it touches. Where there's nothing to bend, the Nursery's cuttings, three to a yard. — Thirty years. It's the one work in the Wold done for nobody.

topic_2.speaker: Kit Laywood
topic_2.text: Because the thorn doesn't like to be slept beside. I can't tell you more than that. Sleep a night against the Briar with no wall between and you'll wake with it round your ankle, and not remember turning over. — So: a ring.

topic_3.speaker: Kit Laywood
topic_3.text: Do not lay thorn anywhere the thorn has not been. — We lay the Briar. We didn't grow it. We don't know what it's for. The Circle says it keeps something out, the Sedgish say it keeps something in, and a layer who thinks she knows is a layer who'll lay it in the wrong place.

hub.speaker: Kit Laywood
hub.text: Go on. The thorn's not going anywhere. That's rather the point.

choices.text: What do the layers do?
Why sleep inside a ring of stone?
What's the rule on your lintel?
You said there's a grey patch that isn't on the thorn.
The stem leaned east with the Nursery's cuttings. It's Briar.
Goodbye.

q_grey_under_the_green_offer.speaker: Kit Laywood
q_grey_under_the_green_offer.text: Half a mile inside the Wold, in the ring of sallows the Hollow cuts its withies from. A forester found it. Grey to the last leaf, the moss and the bracken grey under it to the edge of the ring and no further. She cut a stem and wouldn't carry it. — Countwatch counts the patches on the Briar. They're all on the Briar. This one isn't. — I won't lay thorn round it on my own say. That's the rule. Go and look. Stay the night, if you're braver than the forester. Bring me the stem.

choices.text: I'll go and look.
Not now.

q_grey_under_the_green_accept.speaker: Kit Laywood
q_grey_under_the_green_accept.text: It's due west of the Nursery and a bit north. You'll know it. The colour goes out of the ground like a tide.

q_grey_under_the_green_decide.speaker: Kit Laywood
q_grey_under_the_green_decide.text: *She turns the grey stem over in her gauntlets for a long time.* — Up out of the roots. Half a mile in. Bringing the grey with it. — So the Briar isn't only on the rampart. It's under all of us, and it's come up. — And the rule says don't lay thorn where thorn hasn't been. It has been. It's there. It's just been underneath. — I asked for somebody else's say. You're somebody else. Say.

choices.text: Lay thorn round the ring. The Briar is already there; lay it where it is.
Keep the rule. Put the ring on Countwatch's count and watch it.
Send the stem to the Sayers' Circle. Somebody should find out what the Briar is for.
Let me think on it.

q_grey_under_the_green_decide_lay_it_rou.speaker: Kit Laywood
q_grey_under_the_green_decide_lay_it_rou.text: Where it is. — Yes. That keeps the rule, if you squint, and I'm squinting. Ebb and I will take the Nursery's cuttings in tomorrow and lay a ring round the ring. Whatever's under it can come up inside our thorn instead of the Hollow's withies.

q_grey_under_the_green_decide_leave_it_b.speaker: Kit Laywood
q_grey_under_the_green_decide_leave_it_b.text: Keep it. — The rule's older than me, and I've never broken it, and I don't know what I'd be laying thorn round. We'll put it on the count. Alder Wyke will chalk a new line on the tower: nineteen on the thorn, one inside. And we'll watch it grow.

q_grey_under_the_green_decide_to_the_cir.speaker: Kit Laywood
q_grey_under_the_green_decide_to_the_cir.text: The Circle. — *She hands it back to you like something hot.* — Take it, then. The layers won't carry it. The Sayers will cut it and boil it and write it up, and perhaps they'll find out what it's for, and perhaps they'll tell us. I've laid thorn thirty years without knowing. I'd like to know before I stop.

greetings.text: We laid a ring round the ring. The grey came up to our thorn and stopped. — Ebb says it's leaning on it. I've told him to stop saying things like that.
Nineteen on the thorn and one inside. Alder chalked it on the tower himself and stood looking at it longer than he needed to.
A Sayer wrote from the Spire. Three pages. The last line was 'we do not know either'. I've pinned it to the lintel under the rule.

notes: Kit Laywood's son, a thorn-layer at the Layers' Ring (world life, Briarwold).

greet.speaker: Ebb Laywood
greet.text: Ebb. Laywood, the young one. Mind the bundles, Mum says. She says it to everyone. She says it to me.

topic_1.speaker: Ebb Laywood
topic_1.text: I do, and she says it's a bad habit, and it probably is. — It creaks back. That's all. It's like talking to a ship. — Last month it creaked back before I'd finished.

topic_2.speaker: Ebb Laywood
topic_2.text: In case. — I won't say in case of what. It'd sound daft out loud. It sounds daft in my head.

topic_3.speaker: Ebb Laywood
topic_3.text: It's all thorns. Thirty years of it and look at her face. — I don't mind. Somebody has to, and nobody would, and it turns out I don't mind. Don't tell her. She'd think I'd gone soft.

hub.speaker: Ebb Laywood
hub.text: *He is pinning a runner into the wall's thorn and talking to it.* — Sorry. Yes?

choices.text: Do you talk to the Briar?
Why do you carry a cutting in your shirt?
Is it hard work?
Goodbye.

notes: The bowyer of Stave Hollow (world life, Briarwold), a merchant of bows and strings.

greet.speaker: Aud Yewman
greet.text: *She is flexing a stave across her knee and does not stop.* — Yew, eleven years seasoned, cut in the autumn and not in anger. That's this one. What are you?

topic_1.speaker: Aud Yewman
topic_1.text: Slip the loop off the upper nock. Let the stave come straight. It takes no strength. — It's written on my door for anyone who wants it. The harder part isn't written anywhere: you can feel exactly how much the bow was used. Some come straight like a sigh. Some come straight like a slammed door.

topic_2.speaker: Aud Yewman
topic_2.text: It's true. I went up and looked. — Good gut, well knotted, the way I'd have done it myself. Whoever restrung it knew the craft. — Nobody restrings a hung bow. The hanging's the letting go. Whoever did it hasn't let go of something, and I'd like to know what.

topic_3.speaker: Aud Yewman
topic_3.text: Not your business. — His. He came down the path with it and said he'd taken his last hart and he wanted to hear what it said. So I unstrung it. It came straight slow, like somebody putting a heavy thing down. He cried. Then he went home and had his supper.

hub.speaker: Aud Yewman
hub.text: Buying, asking, or bringing one up to be unstrung?

choices.text: How do you unstring a dead hunter's bow?
Is it true a bow on Hollin Tor was restrung?
Who was the hunter who asked you to unstring his bow while he's alive?
Goodbye.

bye.speaker: Aud Yewman
bye.text: Mind the racks. They're older than you.

notes: The verderer's grandson at the foot of the Verderer's Tower (world life, Briarwold).

greet.speaker: Wat Hurle
greet.text: I'm Wat, he's up there, no he won't come down, yes I've asked, and yes I've got his bread. Hello.

topic_1.speaker: Wat Hurle
topic_1.text: He saw a fire on the far side of the Thornmarch, where there's nothing, and he says he's not coming down till he knows who's tending it. — It's been since the summer. Twice a day, bread up and pot down. I've got very good at ladders.

topic_2.speaker: Wat Hurle
topic_2.text: Once. — He made me lie on my back on the top deck and look where he pointed. It was small. And after the Moot started humming somebody walked away from it with a light, north along the thorn. — I didn't tell Mum.

topic_3.speaker: Wat Hurle
topic_3.text: Grandad's count of fires. He chalks it on the underside of the top deck so you have to lie down to read it. I copied it out down here so I don't have to. It's there, by the ladder. You can read it. Everyone does. Nobody does anything.

hub.speaker: Wat Hurle
hub.text: *He is halfway up the ladder and comes back down it.* — What?

choices.text: Why won't the verderer come down?
Have you seen the fire?
What's the count on the wall?
Goodbye.

bye.speaker: Wat Hurle
bye.text: Mind the third rung. It's the one.

notes: The pit-man at the Sawpit (world life, Briarwold), who has not spoken to his brother on the log above in eleven years.

greet.speaker: Ned Pitt
greet.text: *He looks up out of the pit with one red eye.* — Hup. — Sorry. Habit. What?

topic_1.speaker: Ned Pitt
topic_1.text: Hilde Ashby. — Married a Rafter. Neither of us. Eleven years. — It was never her, if I'm honest. It was him saying it was me that frightened her off, and me saying it was him, and then it was eleven years. The saw does our talking. Hup and pull. It's been a good conversation, for a saw.

topic_2.speaker: Ned Pitt
topic_2.text: Tamwick's carts. The cider comes up the Wold road on our planks and goes down again as barrels on our planks. Good oak, fallen, by the verderers' leave. Nothing cut standing.

topic_3.speaker: Ned Pitt
topic_3.text: *He looks up at the log for a long time.* — No. — Tell him the chalk line's been a hair east all week. He'll know what I mean. It's not a message. It's the line.

hub.speaker: Ned Pitt
hub.text: Make it quick. The saw's waiting and so's he.

choices.text: Why don't you speak to your brother?
What do you saw the planks for?
Is there anything you want carried up to him?
Goodbye.

notes: The top-man at the Sawpit (world life, Briarwold), who has not spoken to his brother in the pit below in eleven years.

greet.speaker: Aldo Pitt
greet.text: *He snaps the chalk line, twice, and looks down into the pit, and back at you.* — Aldo. Top-man. You'll have met the other one.

topic_1.speaker: Aldo Pitt
topic_1.text: Because he started it. — He'll tell you I started it. We're both right, and it was eleven years ago, and the woman married a Rafter and has four children and doesn't remember either of us. — I snap the line twice. The first is always true. The second's in case he says something.

topic_2.speaker: Aldo Pitt
topic_2.text: Who says? — It's a long bench. I moved along for the view. There's a better view of the Vale from the middle. — He hasn't. He's still at his end with his back to me. — That's his business.

topic_3.speaker: Aldo Pitt
topic_3.text: *He looks into the pit a long time.* — Tell him I know about the line. I've been drawing it a hair east on purpose, to see if he'd say. — Don't tell him that. Tell him I know about the line.

hub.speaker: Aldo Pitt
hub.text: Go on. He can't hear us up here. — He can. Go on anyway.

choices.text: Why don't you speak to your brother?
They say you've been eating your bread in the middle of the bench.
Is there anything you want carried down to him?
Goodbye.

bye.speaker: Aldo Pitt
bye.text: Mind the pit. It's deeper than it looks, and he's in it.

notes: The Skarl Delving's hook (world/sites/site_exterior.gd, _hook): the clan's tally-board by the adit. Reads the story; starts core:quest/the_price_at_the_middle for whoever has not had it from Tosk ko-Skarl.

look.speaker: The Skarl tally-board
look.text: A board of larch, the clan's marks burned into it in rows: six hands at the face, tin two baskets, water in the low gallery, the big vein, the big vein. The rows stop. Under them the clan's sign for a debt owed and not paid, and a boy's name in Valish letters, the C of Colley burned backwards. Across all of it one woodfolk notch, cut with a knife, and under that more notches, one a month, the newest fresh. From the adit a draught comes up, cold, smelling of wet stone and something sweetish, and very far down in it, once, a single thin note, as of a whistle badly blown.

choices.text: Follow the note down. Somebody should.
Leave the board as it is.

taken.speaker: The Skarl tally-board
taken.text: The note does not come again. Somebody burns charcoal under the tor; the smoke goes straight up. Somebody stands at the middle of the bridge to the west, too far off to see.

notes: The Horn Pale's hook (world/sites/site_exterior.gd, _hook): the price board at the gate. Reads only; the quest is Corra Bracken's (core:quest/custom_says_wait).

look.speaker: The Horn Pale's price board
look.text: A board painted in a Tallymen's clerk's letters: OROTH ANTLER BOUGHT. Two marks the tine, sealed on the tally. Hinds not bought. Heads before noon. Below it, nailed on later, the sheet a buyer would see in Tollmere, torn from the Ledger of Prices: Oroth antler, the Builders' hand, forty marks the tine. Somebody has drawn a line from the two to the forty in charcoal, and written nothing along it.

choices.text: Ask the Tallying Hide's hunter about the Pale.
Leave the board.

who.speaker: The Horn Pale's price board
who.text: West through the Greatwood, a hide in an oak with a post at its foot cut full of notches. Whoever keeps it has been watching this gate for three summers.

notes: The Layers' Ring's hook (world/sites/site_exterior.gd, _hook): the layers' chalked count on the gate stone. Reads only; the quest is Kit Laywood's.

look.speaker: The layers' count
look.text: Chalked on the gate stone of the ring, in three hands: yards of thorn laid this season, one hundred and ninety. Cuttings planted, six hundred. Gauntlets worn through, four. Layers volunteered, none. And under it, in a fourth hand, larger: GREY PATCH, HALF A MILE IN, THE WITHY RING. NOT ON THE THORN. ASK KIT.

choices.text: Leave the count.

notes: Aud Yewman's grandson and apprentice at Stave Hollow (world life, Briarwold), who carries the dead's bows up Hollin Tor.

greet.speaker: Hob Yewman
greet.text: *He twangs the string of the bow he is carrying, listens, and hums the note back.* — Hob. Yewman. Gran makes them; I string them; I carry them up the tor when it's time.

topic_1.speaker: Hob Yewman
topic_1.text: Heavy, which it shouldn't be; a bow's nothing. — You hang it on a peg in the holly, and you say the words, and you come down, and you don't look back, because if you look back all thousand of them are looking at you. Not at you. At the bow you brought.

topic_2.speaker: Hob Yewman
topic_2.text: *He stops waxing.* — Not me. — I know whose it is. I carried it up myself. It's not my name to say; the Wold doesn't say the names on the tor. — Whoever restrung it used gut from Gran's own reel. I'd know it anywhere; she twists it left. Don't tell her. She'll go up, and her knees won't.

topic_3.speaker: Hob Yewman
topic_3.text: Mostly. Every string's got a note, and everyone's draw stretches it their own way. Corra Bracken's is high and cross. My grandad's was so low it hummed in your teeth. — His is on the tor now. I still hear it when the wind's in the holly.

hub.speaker: Hob Yewman
hub.text: *He is waxing a string between his thumbs.* — Go on.

choices.text: What is it like, carrying a bow up Hollin Tor?
Who restrung the bow on the tor?
Can you tell a hunter by their bowstring?
Goodbye.

bye.speaker: Hob Yewman
bye.text: Mind the stave racks. Gran counts them.
